title: The lymphatic system and innate immunity
blurb: Sort any defense into the first or second line, explain the steps of inflammation, and describe how lymph is collected, filtered and returned to the blood.
question: A day after a splinter goes into a patient's finger, the area is red, warm, swollen and sore, and a lymph node in the armpit feels tender. Which defenses produced these signs, and why is a lymph node in the armpit involved?

teach.body: The body defends itself in three lines. The first two are innate: they are nonspecific, treating every invader the same way, and they act fast. The first line is external barriers that keep pathogens out. The second line is internal: cells and chemicals that attack anything that gets through. The third line is adaptive (acquired) immunity: lymphocytes that target specific invaders and form memory, but take days on a first exposure.

teach.h: The lines of defense in order
teach.caption: Inflammation and fever belong to the second line. They are innate, not adaptive.

head: Barrier
How it protects
rows: Sweep trapped particles out of airways

teach.body: Phagocytes engulf invaders: neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages (from monocytes), plus dendritic cells. Natural killer (NK) cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior exposure. Complement proteins lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis. Interferons, made by virus-infected cells, protect neighboring cells. Fever occurs when pyrogens reset the hypothalamus; a moderate fever inhibits pathogens. Inflammation is the second line's local response.

teach.caption: Loss of function is sometimes listed as a fifth sign. Chemotaxis draws phagocytes in; diapedesis is their squeeze through the vessel wall.

teach.body: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid, now called lymph, and return it to the blood. Flow is one-way, kept moving by valves plus skeletal muscle and breathing movements, because there is no pump. The thoracic duct drains most of the body into the left subclavian vein; the right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax. Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats.

teach.caption: MALT = mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Peyer's patches are in the ileum.
The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ.

teach.h: Scenario: Carlos and the rusty gate
teach.body: Carlos, a pre-nursing student, cuts his hand on a rusty gate, breaching his skin (first line). Mast cells release histamine, so the area turns red, warm, swollen and painful. Neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages (second line). Lymph from the hand drains toward the axillary lymph nodes, which filter it; they swell and feel tender as lymphocytes there begin the third-line response.

teach.text: The SPLEEN filters BLOOD; lymph NODES filter LYMPH. The thoracic duct empties into the LEFT subclavian vein. Inflammation and fever are INNATE (second line), not adaptive. Neutrophils, not macrophages, are usually first on the scene.

items: First line: skin, mucus, cilia, lysozyme, stomach acid, microbiota, flushing.
Second line: neutrophils first, macrophages, NK cells, complement, interferons, fever.
Inflammation: histamine, vasodilation and leaky capillaries, redness, heat, swelling, pain.
Lymph: one-way, valves, no pump; thoracic duct to the left subclavian vein.
Primary organs: bone marrow, thymus. Secondary: nodes (lymph), spleen (blood), MALT.

summary: You can now place any defense in the first, second or third line, list the steps and cardinal signs of inflammation, and name the second-line cells and proteins. You can also trace lymph back to the blood and tell lymph nodes, spleen, thymus and MALT apart.

A.q: Which defense is part of the FIRST line of defense?
options: Lysozyme in tears
Neutrophil phagocytosis
Complement proteins
Natural killer cells
A.why: Tears and saliva contain lysozyme, a surface secretion that attacks bacteria before they get in: a first-line barrier.

whyNot.1: Neutrophils act inside the body once a barrier is breached: second line.
whyNot.2: Complement proteins circulate in the blood: second line.
whyNot.3: NK cells attack infected cells internally: second line.

A.q: Which white blood cells are usually the FIRST phagocytes to arrive at a site of infection?
options: Macrophages
Neutrophils
Natural killer cells
Plasma cells
A.why: Neutrophils are the first phagocytes to reach an infection; macrophages follow.

whyNot.0: Macrophages develop from monocytes and arrive after neutrophils.
whyNot.2: NK cells kill infected and tumor cells but are not the first phagocytes on scene.
whyNot.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies as part of adaptive immunity; they are not phagocytes.

A.q: The thoracic duct returns lymph to the blood by draining into which vessel?
options: Superior vena cava
Right subclavian vein
Left subclavian vein
Inferior vena cava
A.why: The thoracic duct drains most of the body's lymph into the left subclavian vein.

whyNot.0: The superior vena cava receives blood from the subclavian veins downstream, not the thoracic duct directly.
whyNot.1: The right side is served by the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.
whyNot.3: The inferior vena cava drains the lower body's blood; lymph ducts empty in the upper chest.

B.q: Which chemical, released by mast cells and basophils, causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability during inflammation?
options: Interferon
Complement
Pyrogen
Histamine
B.why: Histamine dilates vessels and makes capillaries leaky, producing redness, heat and swelling.

whyNot.0: Interferons are made by virus-infected cells to protect their neighbors.
whyNot.1: Complement proteins lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis; they are blood proteins, not mast cell products.
whyNot.2: Pyrogens reset the hypothalamus to cause fever.

B.q: Which statement about the spleen is CORRECT?
options: It filters lymph and lies in the right upper quadrant
It filters blood and removes old red blood cells
It is the site where T cells mature in childhood
It drains lymph from the right arm and the head
B.why: The spleen, in the left upper quadrant, filters blood, removes old or damaged red cells and platelets, and stores platelets.

whyNot.0: The spleen filters blood, not lymph, and lies in the LEFT upper quadrant.
whyNot.2: T cells mature in the thymus.
whyNot.3: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and right side of the head.

B.q: Interferons are BEST described as proteins that
options: are made by virus-infected cells to protect neighbors
are made by plasma cells to bind specific antigens
punch holes in microbes as part of the complement system
reset the hypothalamus to raise body temperature
B.why: Virus-infected cells release interferons, which help neighboring cells resist the virus.

whyNot.1: Proteins made by plasma cells to bind antigens are antibodies.
whyNot.2: Lysing microbes is the job of complement proteins.
whyNot.3: Resetting the hypothalamus to cause fever is the job of pyrogens.

C.q: Two days after cutting his hand, Carlos notices a tender, swollen lump in his armpit. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: The spleen is filtering lymph drained from the arm
The thymus is making B cells to fight the infection
Axillary nodes are filtering lymph from the hand
Lacteals in the arm are absorbing fats from the wound
C.why: Lymph from the hand drains to the axillary lymph nodes, which filter it and house lymphocytes; they swell during infection.

whyNot.0: The spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it lies in the abdomen, not the armpit.
whyNot.1: B cells mature in red bone marrow; the thymus is where T cells mature.
whyNot.3: Lacteals are in the intestinal villi and absorb dietary fats.

C.q: Which statement about inflammation is CORRECT?
options: It is a specific, adaptive response with memory
Histamine causes vasoconstriction to limit swelling
It is triggered by antibodies made by plasma cells
Its signs are redness, heat, swelling and pain
C.why: Vasodilation and leaky capillaries produce the cardinal signs: redness, heat, swelling and pain.

whyNot.0: Inflammation is innate (second line): nonspecific and without memory.
whyNot.1: Histamine causes vasodilation, which increases swelling.
whyNot.2: Inflammation is started by injury and mediators such as histamine, not by antibodies.

C.q: Natural killer (NK) cells differ from cytotoxic T cells because NK cells
options: kill infected cells with no prior exposure
need antigen presented to them on MHC first
form memory cells after a first infection
are made and then mature in the thymus
C.why: NK cells are innate: they kill virus-infected and tumor cells without needing prior exposure.

whyNot.1: Needing antigen presented on MHC describes T cells, part of adaptive immunity.
whyNot.2: Memory is a feature of adaptive lymphocytes, not innate NK cells.
whyNot.3: Maturing in the thymus describes T cells.

reteach.title: Think of a castle under attack
reteach.question: A castle has walls and a moat, guards who attack any intruder, and trained archers who keep wanted posters of past enemies. Which line of defense is each?

blocks.body: The walls and moat are the first line: skin, mucus and stomach acid simply keep invaders out. The guards are the second line: they attack anyone who climbs in, without asking who they are, just like neutrophils, macrophages and NK cells. Raising the alarm bell is inflammation. The archers with wanted posters are the third line, adaptive immunity: slow to train, but they remember. The drainage ditches with checkpoints are lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes.

blocks.text: The alarm bell is not the archers: inflammation is innate (second line), even though it can call in adaptive cells later.

explain.body: External barriers: intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia, lysozyme in tears and saliva, stomach acid, normal microbiota, flushing by urine, coughing and sneezing.

test.q: Stomach acid protects the body as part of which line of defense?
options: Second line (internal, nonspecific)
Third line (adaptive)
First line (barriers)
Humoral immunity
test.why: Stomach acid destroys swallowed microbes before they enter the tissues: a first-line barrier.

whyNot.0: The second line acts inside the tissues after a barrier is breached.
whyNot.1: The third line is specific adaptive immunity carried out by lymphocytes.
whyNot.3: Humoral immunity is antibody-mediated adaptive immunity, the third line.

explain.body: Phagocytes (neutrophils first, then macrophages), NK cells, complement, interferons and fever. Inflammation: histamine causes vasodilation and leaky capillaries.

test.q: Mast cells release histamine at an injury site. What is the DIRECT effect on nearby capillaries?
options: They constrict and become less permeable
They clot and block local blood flow
They release antibodies into the tissue
They dilate and become more permeable
test.why: Histamine causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, which bring redness, heat and swelling.

whyNot.0: This is the opposite of histamine's effect.
whyNot.1: Histamine increases local blood flow rather than blocking it.
whyNot.2: Antibodies are made by plasma cells, not released by capillaries.

explain.body: Lymph vessels collect excess interstitial fluid and return it to the blood. One-way flow with valves; moved by skeletal muscle and breathing; no pump.

test.q: Which statement about lymph flow is CORRECT?
options: The heart pumps lymph through lymphatic vessels
Valves and muscle movement keep lymph flowing
Lymph flows in a closed loop alongside the arteries
The right lymphatic duct drains most of the body
test.why: Lymphatic vessels have valves for one-way flow, and skeletal muscle and breathing movements push lymph along.

whyNot.0: The lymphatic system has no pump; the heart moves blood, not lymph.
whyNot.2: Lymph flows one way from the tissues back to the veins; it is not a closed loop.
whyNot.3: The thoracic duct drains most of the body; the right lymphatic duct drains the right arm, head and thorax.

explain.body: Primary (lymphocytes mature): red bone marrow and thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes (filter lymph), spleen (filters blood) and MALT (tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix).

test.q: Which are the PRIMARY lymphoid organs?
options: Lymph nodes and spleen
Red bone marrow and thymus
Tonsils and Peyer's patches
Spleen and thymus
test.why: Lymphocytes mature in the primary lymphoid organs: red bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells).

whyNot.0: Lymph nodes and the spleen are secondary lymphoid organs.
whyNot.2: Tonsils and Peyer's patches are MALT, which is secondary lymphoid tissue.
whyNot.3: The thymus is primary, but the spleen is secondary.
